The Board of Public Works oversees state procurement policies and approves significant state contracts. Changes to liability for attorney's fees in procurement disputes directly intersect with state contracting oversight.

The Office of the Attorney General represents state agencies before the MSBCA in bid protests and contract disputes. Increased filings or litigation over reasonable attorney's fees could increase legal workload.

qa_results.bill_summary: Transfers authority to designate a deputy clerk to perform marriage ceremonies from the county administrative judge to the circuit court clerk. Authorizes a deputy clerk designated by the clerk of the circuit court for the county to perform marriages. Maintains existing authority for clerks, judges, and authorized religious officials to perform marriage ceremonies. Takes effect October 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Clerk of the Circuit Court
qa_results.stakeholders: Clerks of the circuit courts, deputy clerks, county administrative judges, and couples marrying in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 300 modifies judicial branch administrative procedures by transferring the authority to designate deputy clerks who may perform marriage ceremonies from the county administrative judges of the circuit courts to the clerks of the circuit court, directly impacting circuit court operations and administration overseen by the Judicial Branch.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Workgroup on Independent Innovation in Prince George's County to promote county innovation and technology. Requires the Urban Business Innovation Initiative within the Maryland Technology Development Corporation to provide staff. Directs the workgroup to recommend investment strategies for industry opportunities and potential areas of innovation. Requires collaboration with local angel investors and stakeholders to foster entrepreneurship and technology start-ups. Requires a final report of recommendations to the General Assembly by January 15, 2026.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Technology Development Corporation; Workgroup on Independent Innovation in Prince George's County
qa_results.stakeholders: Entrepreneurs, technology start-up companies, and angel investors in Prince George's County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures for staffing and workgroup travel reimbursements are minimal and absorbable within existing budgeted resources. Local finances and operations are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Urban Business Innovation Initiative within TEDCO to provide staff support for the newly established Workgroup on Independent Innovation in Prince George's County and requires the workgroup to collaborate with TEDCO.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a temporary state-level workgroup tasked with studying, collaborating with stakeholders, and making policy recommendations regarding technology start-up strategies and innovation in Prince George's County.

The workgroup's statutory membership includes a designated representative from Startup UMD, which is an initiative of the University of Maryland, College Park, a constituent institution of the University System of Maryland.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners to issue a Class C alcoholic beverages license to certain nonprofit organizations. Restricts eligibility to independent and nonprofit nationwide fraternal or sororal organizations meeting specified membership and operating criteria. Excludes college, high school, and student-restricted fraternities and sororities from eligibility. Authorizes the Board to suspend or revoke a license for repeated underage or unauthorized alcohol purchasing violations within one year. Sets the annual license fee at $910.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: independent and nonprofit nationwide fraternal and sororal organizations in Prince George's County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Prince George’s County revenues increase by approximately $5,460 annually beginning in fiscal 2025 from the issuance of six Class C licenses at $910 each. The county can handle additional enforcement using existing budgeted resources. There is no state fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the state's alcoholic beverages industry and enforces state alcohol laws, including the regulation of licensed alcohol wholesalers referenced in the bill's enforcement provisions.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters dispute settlement procedures under the Maryland Cooperative Housing Corporation Act. Requires governing bodies to send written cease and desist demands and hearing notices by certified mail. Increases the minimum abatement period for continuing violations from 10 days to 15 days. Grants members at least 10 days from the notice date to request a hearing. Requires governing bodies to provide at least 10 days' written notice before holding a requested hearing. Directs governing bodies to deliberate on violations and sanctions at their next meeting if no hearing is requested.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary
qa_results.stakeholders: members and governing bodies of cooperative housing corporations in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill modifies the required pre-litigation dispute settlement mechanism for cooperative housing corporations. Decisions rendered through this process may be appealed to Maryland courts, and parties may initiate civil actions for damages or injunctive relief, which directly intersects with court operations.

The Office of the Attorney General, through its Consumer Protection Division, handles consumer disputes and inquiries involving common ownership communities and housing rights, and was consulted in the preparation of the fiscal note.

The Secretary of State maintains regulatory and registry oversight over certain types of common ownership communities (such as condominiums and timeshares) and was consulted as an information source for the bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: Transfers the annual reporting mandate on specified firearm violations from the State Commission on Criminal Sentencing Policy to the Maryland Judiciary. Requires the Maryland Judiciary to report annually to the Governor and General Assembly by October 1, starting in 2024. Specifies that the report must cover charges, convictions, and sentences for wearing, carrying, transporting, or possessing certain regulated firearms. Requires the reported information to be disaggregated by jurisdiction, race, and gender. Takes effect June 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals charged with or convicted of wearing, carrying, or transporting a handgun or unlawful possession of a regulated firearm
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures are not materially affected, as the Maryland Judiciary can implement the reporting requirements with existing budgeted resources. State revenues and local finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 315 requires the Maryland Judiciary to collect, disaggregate by jurisdiction, race, and gender, and annually report data on charges, convictions, and sentences for specified firearm violations to the Governor and the General Assembly. The Administrative Office of the Courts is the operational and data support entity responsible for implementing this reporting requirement.
The bill mandates that the annual report regarding firearm charges, convictions, and sentences be submitted directly to the Governor on or before October 1 each year.

qa_results.bill_summary: Adds the Secretary of Emergency Management and the Chair of the Public Service Commission to the Commission on Climate Change. Authorizes both officials to designate an alternate to serve in their place. Expands the formal statutory membership of the Commission. The Commission advises the Governor and General Assembly on climate change mitigation, preparedness, and adaptation. Takes effect October 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Commission on Climate Change; Maryland Department of the Environment; Maryland Department of Emergency Management; Public Service Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Commission on Climate Change members, Maryland Department of Emergency Management officials, and Public Service Commission officials
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Minimal and absorbable increase in State expenditures for any member expense reimbursements within existing budgeted resources. No local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly adds the Secretary of Emergency Management, or the Secretary's designee, as an official member of the Maryland Commission on Climate Change.
The bill directly adds the Chair of the Public Service Commission, or the Chair's designee, as an official member of the Maryland Commission on Climate Change.
The Commission on Climate Change is established within the Department of the Environment, which also jointly staffs the commission and manages its operations.
The Department of Natural Resources jointly staffs the Maryland Commission on Climate Change alongside the Maryland Department of the Environment.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters the statutory composition of an active state advisory commission, expanding its executive membership.

qa_results.bill_summary: Increases the monetary threshold from $10,000 to $25,000 for transfers requiring court authorization under the Maryland Uniform Transfers to Minors Act. Applies to irrevocable transfers made by a personal representative, trustee, or conservator to a custodian for a minor's benefit. Permits fiduciaries to complete transfers up to $25,000 without obtaining court approval. Requires every transfer to be in the best interest of the minor. Prohibits transfers that conflict with an applicable will, trust agreement, or other governing instrument. Takes effect October 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary; Orphans' Courts
qa_results.stakeholders: personal representatives, trustees, conservators, custodians, and minor beneficiaries in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Register of Wills oversees estate administration, assists personal representatives, and serves as clerk to the Orphans' Court, which handles probate proceedings and petitions regarding estate transfers to custodians for the benefit of minors.

The Administrative Office of the Courts supports the judicial branch, whose courts are responsible for reviewing and authorizing custodial transfers under the Maryland Uniform Transfers to Minors Act when they exceed the statutory threshold.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the statutory definition of an interested person under Maryland estates and trusts law. Establishes that a legatee ceases to be an interested person when their interest is fully paid or adeemed. Adds surviving spouses who timely elect an elective share until the election is withdrawn or ruled ineffective. Includes persons who timely file a petition to caveat a will until the proceeding is disposed of. Excludes assignees of a legatee or an heir from being interested persons.
qa_results.responsible_party: Registers of Wills; Orphans' Courts
qa_results.stakeholders: legatees, surviving spouses electing an elective share, caveat petitioners, assignees of heirs or legatees, and estate personal representatives
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Register of Wills administers probate proceedings and serves as clerk to the Orphans' Court. The definition of 'interested person' directly determines who is entitled to receive notice from the Register of Wills and file petitions in estate and probate matters.

The Administrative Office of the Courts supports the judicial system, including the court proceedings (such as will caveat proceedings, elective share adjudications, and judicial probate) where the statutory rights and standing of 'interested persons' are exercised and adjudicated.

qa_results.bill_summary: Limits who may object to the appointment of a decedent's personal representative to interested persons and unpaid claimants. Alters the required statutory notice of appointment published by the register of wills. Requires eligible objectors to file objections with the register of wills within six months of appointment. Preserves the right of all persons to object to the probate of the decedent's will.
qa_results.responsible_party: Register of Wills
qa_results.stakeholders: Personal representatives, interested persons, and unpaid claimants or creditors of decedents' estates
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Register of Wills is directly responsible for administering estates, having the statutory notice of appointment published in local newspapers, and receiving objections filed against the appointment of personal representatives.

The Administrative Office of the Courts supports the Maryland Judicial Branch, including the Orphans' Courts which adjudicate formal probate matters and contested objections to personal representative appointments.

qa_results.bill_summary: Increases the membership of the Board of Community College Trustees for Anne Arundel County from eight to 10 members. Requires the Governor to appoint the members with the advice and consent of the Senate. Directs the Governor, to the extent practicable, to consider geographic and ethnic representation of Anne Arundel County. Ensures all segments of the county population are represented on the board. Establishes that the terms of the initial additional members begin on July 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Governor; Maryland Senate; Board of Community College Trustees for Anne Arundel County
qa_results.stakeholders: Anne Arundel County residents, students and staff at Anne Arundel Community College, and members of the Board of Community College Trustees for Anne Arundel County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No State fiscal effect. Minimal increase in Anne Arundel Community College expenditures for trustee onboarding, travel reimbursement, and software access, which are likely absorbable with existing resources. No effect on revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill expands the Board of Community College Trustees for Anne Arundel County and directly requires the Governor to appoint two additional members, while taking into account geographic and ethnic representation across the county.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting, vetting, and processing nominations for state and local board appointments, including the new seats added to the Anne Arundel County Board of Community College Trustees.

The Maryland Higher Education Commission coordinates and oversees statewide postsecondary education policies, including the governance structure of Maryland community colleges, and provided information for the bill's fiscal analysis.

qa_results.bill_summary: Modifies requirements for financial assistance policies at acute care and chronic care hospitals under the Health Services Cost Review Commission. Authorizes hospitals to consider only household monetary assets exceeding $100,000 when determining eligibility for free and reduced-cost care. Requires hospitals to exclude tax-preferred retirement assets when evaluating household monetary assets. Removes the requirement that reduced-cost care and payment plans align with a hospital's mission and service area.
qa_results.responsible_party: Health Services Cost Review Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Acute care and chronic care hospitals in Maryland, and uninsured or underinsured patients seeking financial assistance or payment plans for hospital care
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State administrative costs for the Health Services Cost Review Commission can be handled with existing budgeted resources. Potential impacts on Maryland Department of Health chronic care hospitals and the uncompensated care fund are indeterminate but anticipated to be minimal. If hospital rates rise due to uncompensated care adjustments, Medicaid expenditures and matching federal revenues may increase beginning as early as fiscal 2025.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HSCRC directly regulates acute and chronic care hospitals in Maryland, establishes hospital rates, and oversees hospital compliance with statutory financial assistance and uncompensated care policies amended by the bill.

MDH operates state chronic care hospitals (such as Western Maryland Hospital Center and Deer's Head Hospital Center) that are subject to these financial assistance policy standards, and administers the Medicaid program, which could experience expenditure impacts if hospital uncompensated care rate adjustments occur.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Motor Vehicle Administration to report on Maryland residents' motor vehicles improperly titled or registered out-of-state. Mandates consultation with Baltimore City and other interested jurisdictions. Specifies the study must examine relevant laws, resident incentives, enforcement data, insurance effects, and state revenue harms. Requires recommendations regarding enforcement mechanisms, penalties, interstate agreements, and legislative proposals. Mandates submission of findings and recommendations to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Motor Vehicle Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland residents who improperly title or register vehicles out-of-state, Baltimore City, and local jurisdictions
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The Motor Vehicle Administration can prepare and submit the required report using existing resources, and State revenues are not affected. Baltimore City and other participating local governments can assist with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration is the primary agency tasked with preparing, coordinating, and submitting the required comprehensive report on Maryland residents improperly registering vehicles out of state.
The Maryland Department of Transportation is the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration and oversees vehicle administration and transportation policy for the state.
The Motor Vehicle Administration is required to submit the final report containing findings and policy recommendations directly to the Governor.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the State Board of Elections to maintain a website portal for the public to report election misinformation and disinformation. Directs the Board to periodically review submissions, issue corrective information when necessary, or refer matters to the State Prosecutor. Defines election misinformation and disinformation regarding election procedures, results, or voting rights in the State. Expands improper voting influence offenses to include pressure, deception, trickery, or authority, regardless of the medium used. Takes effect June 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections; Office of the State Prosecutor
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland voters; members of the public reporting election misinformation; individuals communicating election information or attempting to influence voters
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least $50,000 in fiscal 2024 to develop and establish the online reporting portal. Special fund revenues for the Fair Campaign Financing Fund may increase beginning in fiscal 2025 from misdemeanor penalties, though the exact amount cannot be reliably estimated. No local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the State Board of Elections with establishing and maintaining a public portal on its website to report election misinformation and disinformation, periodically reviewing submissions, issuing corrective information, and referring potential violations to the State Prosecutor, with an estimated fiscal impact of at least $50,000.

The bill explicitly requires the State Board of Elections to refer relevant submissions of election disinformation and misinformation to the State Prosecutor, who investigates and prosecutes election law violations and improper influence on voting.

The bill amends the definition of improper influence under voting offense statutes carrying misdemeanor penalties and potential civil actions, which fall under the jurisdiction of the state court system.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters geographic boundaries in Baltimore City governing restricted hours of sale for specified alcoholic beverages licensees. Restricts Class B-D-7 licensees within the revised area to sales between 9 a.m. and 10 p.m. Applies the same 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. restrictions to other specified retail license holders. Prohibits extending sales hours in the area if they begin later or end earlier than specified. Takes effect June 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Class B-D-7 license holders and other retail alcoholic beverage licensees operating in the 45th alcoholic beverages district in Baltimore City
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state fiscal effect. Baltimore City can handle any additional enforcement with existing resources, and local revenues are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is tasked with state-level regulation and taxation of the alcohol industry. However, this bill specifically alters local geographic boundaries determining operating hours of sale for Class B-D-7 licenses under the authority of the Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners, having no direct operational or fiscal impact on the state.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the State Treasurer to develop written informational materials regarding the Maryland Achieving a Better Life Experience Program. Mandates providing these materials to the State Board of Education and county boards of education. Requires local school systems to provide the materials to parents at certain IEP, IFSP, and 504 plan meetings. Directs that materials be provided in a parent's native language if that language is not English. Specifies that failure to provide the materials does not constitute grounds for a due process complaint.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Treasurer; Maryland State Board of Education; county boards of education
qa_results.stakeholders: parents and guardians of children with disabilities with Individualized Education Programs, Individualized Family Service Plans, or Section 504 plans; local school systems
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Potential decrease in State and local income tax revenues beginning in FY 2025 due to ABLE account subtraction modifications. State Treasurer nonbudgeted fee revenues and expenditures increase as new accounts are created and distributions occur. Maryland State Department of Education expenditures increase minimally in FY 2025 for tracking system enhancements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 336 directly mandates that the State Treasurer develop written informational materials regarding the Maryland ABLE Program (distributable electronically or by hand) and provide them to the State Board of Education and county boards for distribution during IEP, IFSP, and 504 plan meetings. The Treasurer also administers the ABLE Program and will see nonbudgeted revenue/expenditure changes from new accounts.

The bill amends the Education Article to require the inclusion of Maryland ABLE materials in IEP, IFSP, and 504 plan meetings across public school systems. MSDE is responsible for adopting related regulations and updating student tracking systems to monitor document distribution compliance.

Maryland 529 manages the Maryland ABLE program under the oversight of the State Treasurer's Office. It maintains existing informational materials and manages the accounts, contributions, and qualified disability expense distributions impacted by the bill.

The bill is projected to reduce state income tax revenues collected by the Comptroller due to an increase in personal income tax subtraction modifications claimed for contributions to and distributions from newly opened ABLE accounts.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits drivers from failing to yield the right-of-way to persons lawfully riding in a designated bike lane or shoulder. Applies when the failure to yield contributes to the serious physical injury or death of a rider. Covers individuals riding a bicycle, an electric personal assistive mobility device, or a motor scooter. Subjects convicted violators to imprisonment not exceeding two months, a maximum fine of $2,000, or both. Takes effect October 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Judiciary
qa_results.stakeholders: Drivers of motor vehicles and persons riding bicycles, electric personal assistive mobility devices, or motor scooters in designated bike lanes or shoulders
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $56,900 in FY 2025 only for Judicial computer programming changes. State revenues and local finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Judiciary, requiring $56,900 in general fund expenditures in FY 2025 for judicial system programming changes to track and adjudicate the new misdemeanor penalty.

As the agency responsible for driver licensing, driving records, and the assessment of points for moving violations under the Maryland Vehicle Law, MVA must record convictions and assess points for violations of this updated statute.

The bill amends the Transportation Article regarding vehicle right-of-way laws in bike lanes and shoulders, falling directly within MDOT's overarching jurisdiction over state transportation rules and safety.

MSP is the primary statewide law enforcement agency responsible for enforcing motor vehicle laws, conducting traffic stops, and investigating serious traffic collisions involving bicycles, EPAMDs, or scooters.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes criminal misdemeanor penalties including imprisonment for up to two months, touching on the state's correctional and criminal justice administration.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes requirements, procedures, and prohibitions governing the use of facial recognition technology by law enforcement agencies. Limits law enforcement use of facial recognition technology in criminal investigations to specified offenses and ongoing public safety threats. Prohibits introducing facial recognition results in court proceedings except for probable cause or positive identification in preliminary matters. Requires the Department of State Police to adopt and publish a model statewide policy. Requires law enforcement agencies using the technology to complete annual audits and mandatory annual training. Authorizes individuals to bring a civil action against a law enforcement agency to compel compliance.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of State Police; Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services; Governor's Office of Crime Prevention, Youth, and Victim Services
qa_results.stakeholders: State and local law enforcement agencies, criminal defendants, juveniles subject to delinquency proceedings, and individuals investigated using facial recognition technology
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least $474,100 in fiscal 2025 and reach $579,200 by fiscal 2029 for staff to develop and administer mandatory training and compile annual statewide reports. Local law enforcement agencies face operational impacts and potential training costs, while local revenues are unaffected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is mandated to develop and administer a mandatory annual training program regarding the use of facial recognition technology in criminal investigations by June 30, 2026. The department also operates the Maryland Image Repository System (MIRS) and incurs significant fiscal expenditures for staff and technology.

The Department of State Police is statutorily required to adopt and publish a model statewide policy governing the use of facial recognition technology by law enforcement agencies, and must comply with the bill's investigative restrictions, training, auditing, and reporting mandates.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is mandated to receive annual facial recognition technology reports from all law enforcement agencies across the state and compile and submit an annual disaggregated report to the Governor and General Assembly, requiring additional personnel expenditures.
The bill explicitly limits facial recognition image comparisons primarily to the database of driver's license and identification card photos maintained by the Motor Vehicle Administration.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes evidentiary exclusions, strict probable cause standards, and mandatory discovery disclosure requirements for facial recognition evidence in criminal and juvenile delinquency cases, and specifically authorizes the Public Defender to request and inspect annual law enforcement compliance audits.

The bill creates rules and limitations regarding the admissibility of facial recognition results in criminal and juvenile delinquency court proceedings, limits evidence for warrants and preliminary hearings, and authorizes civil actions in court to compel law enforcement compliance.

The Attorney General is explicitly authorized under the bill to receive and review annual facial recognition audit materials upon request and provides legal counsel regarding evidentiary rules, civil actions, and agency compliance.

MDOT oversees the Motor Vehicle Administration, whose photo database is specified for facial recognition comparisons, and operates law enforcement units that must comply with the bill's operational, training, audit, and reporting mandates.

DNR operates the Maryland Natural Resources Police, a law enforcement agency directly subject to the bill's restrictions on facial recognition technology use, training mandates, annual audits, and reporting requirements.

DGS houses the Maryland Capitol Police, which constitutes a law enforcement agency subject to the bill's operational limits, mandatory training, annual compliance audits, and reporting obligations regarding facial recognition technology.

MDTA maintains its own accredited police force, which is subject to the bill's restrictions on the use of facial recognition technology, mandatory DPSCS training, compliance audits, and annual reporting.
The Governor's Office receives the annual statewide report from GOCPP detailing law enforcement use of facial recognition technology.

qa_results.bill_summary: Extends State procurement prompt payment requirements and dispute resolution procedures to suppliers providing labor or materials to contractors. Requires contractors to pay suppliers undisputed amounts within 10 days of receiving payment from the State. Authorizes suppliers to submit written notice of nonpayment to the designated procurement officer. Authorizes unit representatives to withhold progress payments to delinquent contractors or assess penalties up to $100 per day. Authorizes contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers to appeal certain delinquency decisions to the procurement officer.
qa_results.responsible_party: State procurement units and procurement officers
qa_results.stakeholders: Contractors holding State procurement contracts and suppliers providing labor or materials to those contractors
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state or local fiscal impact. State agencies can implement the dispute resolution and prompt payment requirements using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's central procurement authority, DGS oversees state purchasing and contracting procedures. Its procurement officers and unit representatives are directly tasked with incorporating the prompt payment clauses and administering dispute resolution procedures between contractors and suppliers.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state procurement contracts and regulations under the State Finance and Procurement Article, making the expansion of prompt payment requirements to suppliers directly relevant to its governance.

MDOT manages extensive capital, highway, and infrastructure contracts involving numerous contractors and material suppliers. Its procurement officers must enforce the bill's prompt payment dispute and penalty provisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Board of Contract Appeals
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSBCA adjudicates disputes between state contractors and vendors under State procurement law; although prompt payment decisions under this specific section have statutory limits on review, the board monitors procurement dispute statutory frameworks.
DBM exercises executive oversight over state spending, procurement policy, and budget execution across executive branch agency contracts.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Department of the Environment to approve redepositing dredged material at the Hart-Miller Island facility through December 31, 2027. Requires dredging operators to enter into an approved community benefits agreement with Baltimore County before receiving approval. Authorizes the Department to approve contained redeposit areas at large redevelopment sites near Hart-Miller Island. Prohibits the approval of dredged material redeposit using confined aquatic disposal within five miles of the island chain. Alters the membership and advisory duties of the Cox Creek Citizens Oversight Committee regarding dredged material management. Expands the monitoring duties of the Hart-Miller-Pleasure Island Citizens Oversight Committee to include community benefits agreements.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment; Maryland Port Administration; Board of Public Works
qa_results.stakeholders: Residents and waterfront communities near Hart-Miller Island and Cox Creek, Baltimore County, commercial dredging project operators, and industrial port developers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State operational and maintenance costs may increase significantly if the Hart-Miller Island facility reopens, though costs are intended to be offset by per-cubic-yard user fees. Baltimore County revenues and expenditures may increase significantly from payments under required community benefits agreements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDE is granted regulatory authority under the bill to approve contained areas for the redeposit of dredged material at large redevelopment sites and to approve the redeposit of dredged material at the Hart-Miller Island Dredged Material Containment Facility under specified statutory conditions.

MPA manages the State's Dredged Material Management Program; the bill specifically alters the statutory duties of the Cox Creek Citizens Oversight Committee to advise, provide feedback, and make recommendations directly to MPA regarding containment facility operations.
MDOT is the parent department of the Maryland Port Administration, which oversees dredging programs and dredged material containment facilities impacted by the legislation.

The bill statutorily authorizes the Board of Public Works to approve a wetlands license or license amendment permitting the deposit of dredged material at the Hart-Miller Island Dredged Material Containment Facility.

DNR owns Hart-Miller Island and operates a State park on the southern portion of the island, which could experience operational and financial impacts if the dredged material containment facility is reopened.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies the composition, oversight scope, and statutory responsibilities of the Cox Creek Citizens Oversight Committee and the Hart-Miller-Pleasure Island Citizens Oversight Committee.
MES provides operational and technical support for dredging and dredged material containment facilities under contract to MPA and may be involved should operations at containment facilities expand.
The Governor is statutorily tasked with appointing members and establishing terms for both the Cox Creek Citizens Oversight Committee and the Hart-Miller-Pleasure Island Citizens Oversight Committee.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting, vetting, and processing appointments for the altered seats on the Cox Creek Citizens Oversight Committee.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the definitions of fish and wildlife under State conservation laws to include invertebrates and animal products. Requires petitions proposing to add or remove endangered or threatened species to submit specified biological data and documentation. Requires the Secretary of Natural Resources to review and, if warranted, update endangered and threatened species regulations. Mandates these regulatory reviews on or before July 1, 2026, and at least every five years thereafter. Excludes federal Endangered Species Act listings from the State petition review requirement.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources; Secretary of Natural Resources
qa_results.stakeholders: Petitioners proposing species listings or delistings, wildlife conservation organizations, researchers, and individuals or entities regulated by Maryland fish and wildlife protection laws
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state or local fiscal effect. The Department of Natural Resources can implement the bill with existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 345 directly tasks the Secretary of Natural Resources and the Department of Natural Resources with reviewing and updating regulations that list endangered and threatened species of fish and wildlife at least every five years, handling petitions to list or delist species according to new statutory requirements, and enforcing updated definitions of 'fish' and 'wildlife'.

qa_results.bill_summary: Redefines the Health and Human Services Referral System as a coordinated resource system accessible through 2-1-1 and other technology systems. Clarifies that 2-1-1 Maryland administers the statewide 2-1-1 system. Repeals requirements that the Maryland Department of Health evaluate call center performance and recommend corrective actions. Removes the department's duty to make recommendations regarding call center service quality. Requires 2-1-1 Maryland call centers to nominate two representatives by July 1, 2024, for the governing board of directors.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland residents seeking health and human services resources, 2-1-1 Maryland, and 2-1-1 Maryland call centers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Any change in State activities does not materially affect State finances. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies the statutory responsibilities of the Maryland Department of Health by repealing requirements that the department evaluate the performance of 2-1-1 Maryland call centers and issue recommendations regarding service quality and corrective actions.

As the primary state department administering human services, the Department of Human Services is directly connected to the Health and Human Services Referral System and must consult with 2-1-1 Maryland if establishing public information telephone lines or hotlines.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Workgroup on Health and Wellness in Prince George's County. Requires the Prince George's County Health Officer to designate the chair. Requires the Prince George's County Health Department to provide staff for the Workgroup. Directs the Workgroup to evaluate health practices, integrative wellness programs, and healthy eating initiatives. Requires recommendations on community programming best practices and incentives for employers, businesses, and county agencies. Mandates a final report of findings and recommendations to state and county officials by December 1, 2025.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County Health Department; Prince George's County Health Officer
qa_results.stakeholders: Prince George's County residents, local health and wellness businesses, integrative health practitioners, and Prince George's County government agencies
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state fiscal effect. Prince George's County expenditures increase by approximately $120,000 in FY 2025 and FY 2026 to hire one contractual employee to staff the workgroup and prepare the report.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 358 establishes a temporary statutory body, the Workgroup on Health and Wellness in Prince George's County, to study community health programming and make recommendations before sunsetting in 2026.
The bill requires the Workgroup on Health and Wellness in Prince George's County to submit its final report of findings and recommendations to the Governor on or before December 1, 2025.

The Maryland Department of Health oversees local health departments across the state; the bill tasks the Prince George's County Health Officer with designating the workgroup chair and the Prince George's County Health Department with providing staff.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a barbershop and beauty salon beer and wine license in Caroline County. Authorizes the Board of License Commissioners for Caroline County to issue the license to eligible permit holders. Allows licensees to provide up to 12 ounces of beer or 5 ounces of wine to customers. Restricts service to customers actively receiving barbering or cosmetology services during normal business hours. Prohibits license holders from transferring the license to another location. Establishes an annual license fee of $100 and requires alcohol awareness training.
qa_results.responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Caroline County
qa_results.stakeholders: Caroline County barbershop permit holders, beauty salon permit holders, and their customers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Caroline County revenues increase minimally by $100 annually for each license issued, though total revenue cannot be reliably estimated. Local monitoring and enforcement can be absorbed with existing resources. No material impact on State operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor oversees professional and occupational licensing boards under the Business Occupations and Professions Article, including permits for barbershops and beauty salons referenced by the bill.
The Comptroller of Maryland oversees state alcohol regulation and taxation, although this license is administered at the local county level by the Caroline County Board of License Commissioners.

qa_results.bill_summary: Expands the one-day beer and wine tasting license in Caroline County to include liquor tasting. Authorizes the Caroline County Board of License Commissioners to issue the license to qualified organizations. Permits individuals to consume up to 0.5 ounces of liquor per offering and 2.5 ounces daily. Increases the daily consumption limit for beer tastings from 8 ounces to 9 ounces. Prohibits charging consumers for tastings and requires consumption on the licensed premises.
qa_results.responsible_party: Caroline County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage licensees, qualifying organizations, and event attendees in Caroline County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state fiscal effect. Caroline County operations and revenues are not anticipated to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the state's alcohol industry and oversees state alcohol laws and excise tax collection. While this bill specifically addresses local per diem tasting licenses administered by the Caroline County Board of License Commissioners with no state fiscal impact, it falls within the broad subject area of alcohol regulation.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the use of stop sign monitoring systems in school zones in Prince George's County. Limits the placement of stop sign monitoring systems to 10 total systems countywide. Requires the Prince George's County Council to approve all monitoring camera locations. Subjects vehicle owners or drivers recorded violating stop sign laws to a civil penalty up to $40. Prohibits contractor compensation from being calculated on a per-ticket basis. Mandates an evaluation report to the General Assembly by December 1, 2025.
qa_results.responsible_party: District Court of Maryland; State Highway Administration; Motor Vehicle Administration; Prince George's County Department of Public Works and Transportation
qa_results.stakeholders: Motor vehicle owners and drivers in Prince George's County; Prince George's County law enforcement agencies and municipalities; school zone pedestrians
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $11,100 in FY 2025 for District Court computer programming. Potential indeterminate increases in local revenues and State fine revenues from citations from FY 2025 through FY 2029, offset by local implementation and operational expenses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The District Court has exclusive original civil jurisdiction over contested citations resulting from stop sign monitoring systems under the bill. The Chief Judge of the District Court is required to prescribe a uniform citation form and adopt trial and penalty collection procedures, resulting in an estimated $11,100 in programming costs in FY 2025.

The State Highway Administration must authorize the deployment of any stop sign monitoring systems on State highways in Prince George's County school zones and is required to prominently install signage providing notice of the systems on State highways, impacting Transportation Trust Fund expenditures.

As the parent agency overseeing the State Highway Administration and Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT's Transportation Trust Fund finances SHA's required signage installation and planning for state highway deployments.

The bill authorizes the Motor Vehicle Administration to refuse registration or reregistration, or suspend registration, for motor vehicles with unpaid and uncontested civil penalties under the monitoring system.

The Prince George's County Department of Public Works and Transportation is mandated to submit a comprehensive implementation and evaluation report on the stop sign monitoring program to the Governor by December 1, 2025.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires each community college to develop and implement a plan providing students access to over-the-counter contraception. Mandates completion of the plan by August 1, 2025, in consultation with students and student organizations. Directs institutions to provide 24-hour access via health centers, retail establishments, vending machines, or other campus methods. Requires each community college to report annually on plan implementation to the Maryland Higher Education Commission. Requires the Commission to submit an annual report on the collected information to the General Assembly. Authorizes the Maryland Department of Health to provide technical assistance to community colleges upon request.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission; Maryland Department of Health; Baltimore City Community College
qa_results.stakeholders: Community college students, student organizations, Baltimore City Community College, and local community colleges across Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Expenditures for Baltimore City Community College and local community colleges may increase, particularly in fiscal 2025 and 2026 for one-time setup costs such as purchasing vending machines. Higher education revenues may increase minimally to offset costs if student fees are charged. The Maryland Department of Health can handle authorized technical assistance with existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHEC is directly tasked with administering reporting requirements under the bill. It must provide the reporting form to community colleges, collect annual implementation reports from them, and submit an annual summary report to the Maryland General Assembly.

qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals at risk of opioid overdose, healthcare providers dispensing overdose reversal drugs, and the Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health can complete and submit the required reports using existing budgeted resources. There is no effect on State revenues or local finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) to report annually to the General Assembly by December 1 in 2024, 2025, and 2026 on FDA-approved opioid overdose reversal drugs and whether MDH has added each drug to a statewide standing order.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System to pay earned incentives to the Chief Investment Officer. Permits this incentive payout if the officer retires directly from the Investment Division on or within 30 days after separation. Clarifies that an age-60 limit on extending Deferred Retirement Option Program participation applies only to State Police Retirement System members. Removes the accidental application of the age-60 Deferred Retirement Option Program extension cap to Law Enforcement Officers' Pension System members. Takes effect July 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System
qa_results.stakeholders: Chief Investment Officer of the State Retirement and Pension System, members of the State Police Retirement System, and members of the Law Enforcement Officers' Pension System
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state or local fiscal impact. The bill makes technical and clarifying adjustments that have no effect on pension liabilities, contribution rates, or revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly governs the administration of the State Retirement and Pension System, authorizing the Board of Trustees to pay incentive compensation to the Chief Investment Officer upon retirement and clarifying DROP participation rules.

The bill clarifies age restrictions and extension procedures for State Police Retirement System members participating in the Deferred Retirement Option Program (DROP), requiring signed acknowledgment by the Director of Human Resources within the Department of State Police.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Maryland Center for School Safety to collaborate with a research entity to study active shooter drills and trainings. Prohibits active shooter drills and trainings from including simulated gunfire sounds, explosion noises, and live role-playing exercises. Excludes voluntary after-school drills or trainings from these trauma-sensitive drill restrictions. Requires local school systems to announce drills in advance, notify parents, and provide mental health follow-up. Requires local school systems to collect and report drill effectiveness and psychological impact data to the Center. Directs the Center to create model safe firearm storage content for annual distribution to parents.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Center for School Safety; Maryland State Department of Education; Department of State Police
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland public school students, parents and guardians, public school personnel, and local school systems
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $200,000 in FY 2025 and by $100,000 annually thereafter to contract with a research entity for data collection and analysis. Local school system expenditures may increase by an indeterminate amount to provide required mental health follow-up to students and school personnel.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MCSS is the primary implementing agency tasked with collaborating with a research institution to study active shooter drill impacts, establishing drill best practices, adjudicating trauma-sensitive drill components, and developing model firearm storage content.

MSDE is authorized to adopt regulations incorporating drills or trainings into the annual school drill schedule, is required to annually review MCSS best practices to update drills, and consults with MCSS on trauma-sensitive requirements.
The bill explicitly requires MCSS to consult with the Department of State Police to develop model content informing parents of Maryland's firearm storage laws.

The bill requires MCSS to collaborate with an institution of higher education to conduct research and data analysis on the effectiveness and psychological impact of active shooter drills, which may involve contracting with USM institutions.
MSDE is required by statute to notify the Governor of proposed regulatory changes that alter the annual schedule of public school safety drills.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the composition and responsibilities of the Maryland Efficient Grant Application Council. Adds the Comptroller to the Council and designates the Secretary of Budget and Management as chair. Removes the Governor's Grants Office from statutory Council duties and transfers technical assistance responsibilities to the Department. Requires the Council to study creating a State Grants Ombudsperson and report recommendations by July 1, 2025. Extends the deadline for the Council's full recommendations report to July 1, 2027. Extends the termination date of the Council by four years to June 30, 2029.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Budget and Management; Maryland Efficient Grant Application Council
qa_results.stakeholders: State grant-making agencies, grant applicants, and nonprofit grant recipients in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No effect on State or local revenues or expenditures. Council members can carry out staffing responsibilities and conduct the required study with existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Secretary of Budget and Management (or designee) as the Chair of the Maryland Efficient Grant Application Council, tasks the department with providing technical assistance and policy interpretations, directs the Council's recommendations to DBM, and requires DBM to report regularly to the General Assembly.

The bill directly removes the Governor's Grants Office from the Maryland Efficient Grant Application Council and reassigns all of its previous statutory duties, including serving as chair and receiving recommendations, to the Department of Budget and Management.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the composition, duties, reporting requirements, and termination date of the Maryland Efficient Grant Application Council, an executive advisory council.
The bill officially adds the Comptroller of Maryland (or the Comptroller's designee) as a statutory member of the Maryland Efficient Grant Application Council.

The Governor is responsible for appointing and having removal authority over five nonprofit representatives to the Council, and the legislation reflects the executive branch realignment of grant coordination priorities.
The State Treasurer (or designee) is designated as a statutory member of the Council, sharing in its staffing and advisory responsibilities.
The Attorney General (or designee) serves as a statutory member of the Council, sharing in its staffing and advisory duties.
The Chief Procurement Officer (or designee), housed within DGS, serves as a statutory member of the Council and shares in its staffing and operational duties.

The Secretary of Health (or designee) is a statutory member of the Council, and as a major grant-making agency, MDH must maintain a Chief Accountability Officer to coordinate with the Council and DBM.
The Secretary of Human Services (or designee) is a statutory member of the Council, and the department must participate as a grant-making agency in the implementation of uniform grant requirements.
The Secretary of Housing and Community Development (or designee) serves as a member of the Council and must provide a Chief Accountability Officer liaison for state grant reform.
The Secretary of Agriculture (or designee) is a statutory member of the Council, participating in recommendations regarding statewide grant processes and uniform guidance.
The Secretary of the Environment (or designee) serves on the Council and must coordinate through its Chief Accountability Officer regarding grant administration reform.
The State Superintendent of Schools (or designee) serves as a statutory member of the Council representing public education grant-making and administration.
The Director of the Maryland Energy Administration (or designee) serves as a statutory member of the Council.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Executive Director of the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention, Youth, and Victim Services (now GOCPP) serves as a statutory member of the Council.
The Chair of the Maryland Higher Education Commission (or designee) is a statutory member of the Council.
The Secretary of Natural Resources (or designee) is a statutory member of the Council, sharing in its staffing and grant reform advisory duties.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Maryland Recreation Communication Boards Pilot Program within the Department of Natural Resources. Requires the Department to construct communication boards in newly constructed State park play areas, subject to available funding. Requires local governing bodies receiving pilot grants to construct at least one communication board in each new play area. Authorizes the Department and local governing bodies to install communication boards when altering existing play areas. Limits grant awards to local governing bodies to $3,000 for each communication board purchased and installed. Authorizes up to $100,000 from the Park System Capital Improvements and Acquisition Fund for the pilot program.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources
qa_results.stakeholders: Children and individuals with limited language skills; the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission; county governing bodies and Baltimore City; playground equipment vendors and contractors.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No net effect on overall State finances, as up to $100,000 is reallocated from existing resources in the Park System Capital Improvements and Acquisition Fund to support the pilot program through fiscal 2028. Local revenues and expenditures may increase by up to $100,000 collectively from grants, with potential additional local expenditures if communication board costs exceed the $3,000 grant limit per board.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) with administering the Maryland Recreation Communication Boards Pilot Program, constructing communication boards in newly constructed play areas under its jurisdiction, awarding grants of up to $3,000 per board to local governing bodies, allocating up to $100,000 from the Park System Capital Improvements and Acquisition Fund, and submitting interim and final evaluation reports to the General Assembly.

The bill directly relates to accessibility and inclusive accommodations in public recreational spaces for individuals with disabilities and communication limitations. The Department of Disabilities coordinates statewide disability access policies and provided subject matter information during the evaluation of the legislation.

qa_results.bill_summary: Repeals requirements for the Housing Opportunities Commission of Montgomery County to hold public hearings on proposed assisted family housing. Eliminates the mandates to report written hearing findings and advertise hearings in two county newspapers. Repeals the requirement to publish a summary of the annual financial report in at least two county newspapers. Maintains the requirement that the Commission publish its annual financial report and certified audit report on its website. Takes effect October 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Housing Opportunities Commission of Montgomery County
qa_results.stakeholders: Housing Opportunities Commission of Montgomery County; residents seeking or residing in assisted family housing in Montgomery County; local newspapers in Montgomery County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state fiscal effect. The bill is not anticipated to materially affect Montgomery County operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Housing and Community Development Article regarding public hearing and reporting requirements for the Housing Opportunities Commission of Montgomery County. While DHCD is the primary state housing agency and provided information on the bill, the changes apply strictly to local Montgomery County housing operations with no state fiscal impact.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires motion picture houses to provide access to operational closed movie captioning technology for screenings available with closed captioning. Requires entities operating a motion picture house with eight or more screens to provide open movie captioning. Mandates at least two open-captioned screenings per movie each week during the first three weeks after premiere. Exempts motion pictures screened fewer than five times from Friday through Thursday in a seven-day period. Authorizes these motion picture houses to provide open movie captioning with reasonable notice beginning three weeks after premiere.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Commission on Civil Rights
qa_results.stakeholders: Motion picture house owners and operators in Maryland, and movie theater patrons who are deaf, hard of hearing, or use captioning
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No material state or local fiscal impact. The Maryland Commission on Civil Rights can handle any additional complaints generated by the bill using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Commission on Civil Rights enforces the state's public accommodation laws under Title 20 of the State Government Article and will be responsible for handling complaints regarding movie theater captioning compliance.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency advocates for equal access and public accommodations for Deaf and hard of hearing residents, who are the direct beneficiaries of mandatory closed and open movie captioning.
The department coordinates policies to advance accessibility and inclusion across the state for individuals with disabilities, aligning directly with the bill's public accommodation requirements.

The Administrative Office of the Courts was consulted as an information source and provides support for any judicial appeals or civil actions arising under public accommodation discrimination provisions.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Rental Assistance for Community School Families Program and Fund to support eligible student households. Requires the Department of Housing and Community Development to administer the program in consultation with the State Department of Education. Authorizes assistance for rent, utilities, related fees, arrears, and relocation expenses. Limits household support to 12 months, with a possible three-month extension subject to funding availability. Authorizes the Governor to include a $10,000,000 appropriation for the fund in the fiscal year 2026 budget bill.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Housing and Community Development; Maryland State Department of Education
qa_results.stakeholders: eligible student households at community schools experiencing housing instability, landlords, utility providers, and community school coordinators
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $5.0 million in FY 2025, budgeted contingent on the bill's enactment, and special fund revenues and expenditures increase by $6.3 million (including $1.3 million from a contingent court surcharge distribution). Discretionary funding in out-years could increase general fund expenditures by $10.0 million annually beginning in FY 2026, with special fund revenues and expenditures increasing by $11.7 million annually. No local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DHCD is the primary agency designated to administer the Rental Assistance for Community School Families Program and the newly established special fund.

MSDE is required to consult with DHCD on program administration, and its Director of Community Schools and local community school coordinators assist in identifying eligible households and coordinating wraparound rental assistance.

The bill explicitly mandates coordination between MSDE's Director of Community Schools and the Governor's Office for Children to support outreach and implementation of State programs for children in community schools.

The State Treasurer is statutorily required to hold the new Rental Assistance for Community School Families Fund separately and oversee the retention of interest earnings under the State Finance and Procurement Article.
The Comptroller is statutorily designated to account for the new Rental Assistance for Community School Families Fund.
The bill authorizes the Governor to include an annual discretionary appropriation of up to $10,000,000 in the State budget for the fund.
DBM oversees the state budget execution and fiscal planning associated with the contingent $5 million FY 2025 allocation and future discretionary appropriations of $10 million.

qa_results.bill_summary: Renames the Department of Veterans Affairs to be the Department of Veterans and Military Families. Renames the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to be the Secretary of Veterans and Military Families. Requires the Secretary to appoint a Deputy Secretary of Military Family Policy and Programs. Directs the deputy secretary to oversee policy and programs related to military families. Prohibits using new letterhead and printed documents until existing supplies are fully depleted.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Veterans and Military Families
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland veterans and military families
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $178,600 in FY 2025 to hire the new deputy secretary and purchase renaming supplies. Annual ongoing expenditures range from $170,300 in FY 2026 to $193,600 in FY 2029. Local operations and finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly renames the Department of Veterans Affairs to the Department of Veterans and Military Families, creates a new position for a Deputy Secretary of Military Family Policy and Programs, and incurs direct fiscal and operational impacts for the department.

The Governor oversees the executive branch departments, including cabinet-level reorganizations, and appoints the Secretary of Veterans and Military Families with the advice and consent of the Senate.

qa_results.bill_summary: Replaces references to mental retardation with intellectual disability across the Courts and Judicial Proceedings and Criminal Procedure Articles. Defines intellectual disability as a developmental disability evidenced by significantly below average intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior impairment. Updates competency evaluations, commitment standards, and conditional release provisions in juvenile and criminal proceedings. Modifies pleas of not criminally responsible to cite a mental disorder or an intellectual disability instead of insanity. Clarifies that the changes do not disturb decisional law interpreting mental retardation or insanity. Takes effect October 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary; Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Juveniles and adult criminal defendants with intellectual disabilities, defense counsel, and prosecutors
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state or local fiscal impact; the bill is technical in nature and has no effect on governmental operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill updates statutory terminology referencing the Maryland Department of Health and its Developmental Disabilities Administration regarding inpatient care, competency evaluations, and court-ordered commitments for individuals with intellectual disabilities.

The bill makes technical corrections to the Courts and Judicial Proceedings and Criminal Procedure Articles, affecting statutory terminology used by the judiciary in competency determinations, criminal responsibility pleas, and commitment orders.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill updates legal standards and terminology in the Criminal Procedure and Courts and Judicial Proceedings Articles governing pleas of not criminally responsible, competency to stand trial, and juvenile competency proceedings handled by defense counsel.

The bill amends provisions in Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article Title 3, Subtitle 8A governing juvenile court proceedings, competency attainment, and commitments for youth involved in the juvenile justice system.

As the state agency responsible for coordinating services and policy for residents with disabilities, the department is directly aligned with legislative updates modernizing statutory references from 'mental retardation' to 'intellectual disability.'

qa_results.bill_summary: Exempts qualified 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations from filing a statement of political contributions with the State Board of Elections. Applies to entities that spend at least $500 to compensate one or more regulated lobbyists. Relieves eligible nonprofits from reporting political contributions and the lobbyists they employ or retain. Takes effect July 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Elections
qa_results.stakeholders: nonprofit organizations qualified under § 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code that compensate regulated lobbyists
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly exempts 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations from having to file statements of political contributions with the State Board of Elections when providing lobbyist compensation.
The bill amends the lobbying provisions of the Maryland Public Ethics Law (General Provisions Article, Title 5, Subtitle 7), which the State Ethics Commission oversees and enforces.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters provisions governing the calculation and modification of child support for incarcerated obligors. Authorizes courts to determine that incarceration constitutes a material change of circumstance warranting child support modification. Prohibits courts from considering an incarcerated parent voluntarily impoverished or imputing potential income to that parent. Repeals the 180-day minimum sentence requirement for suspending child support arrearage accrual during incarceration. Halts arrearage accrual during confinement and for 60 days after release if the obligor lacks resources.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Human Services; Maryland Judiciary
qa_results.stakeholders: Incarcerated child support obligors and child support obligees
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $124,800 in FY 2025 only for one-time computer programming costs for the Department of Human Services. Local finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This departmental bill was requested by the Department of Human Services (DHS) to align state law with federal child support standards. DHS Child Support Administration directly oversees Title IV-D child support accounts and will implement changes to adjust incarcerated obligor payment accounts, incurring $124,800 in one-time IT programming costs.

The bill alters judicial standards and procedures under the Family Law Article for modifying child support awards and calculating obligations when a obligor is incarcerated, impacting Maryland state court proceedings.

qa_results.bill_summary: Codifies the Maryland Zero Emission Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Council in the Transportation Article. Expands Council membership to include the Secretary of General Services and an automotive dismantler and recycler. Separates plug-in electric drive vehicle manufacturer representation into distinct light-duty and heavy-duty categories. Requires the Maryland Department of Transportation, assisted by other state agencies, to provide staff support. Mandates interim progress reports in 2024 and 2025, followed by a final report by June 30, 2026. Terminates the Council and its codified statutory provisions on June 30, 2026.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Zero Emission Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Council; Maryland Department of Transportation; Maryland Energy Administration; Maryland Public Service Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Zero-emission and electric vehicle manufacturers, automotive dismantlers and recyclers, electric companies, retail electric suppliers, fleet vehicle operators, and electric vehicle drivers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state or local fiscal impact, as codifying the Council and altering its membership does not affect governmental finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDOT is the primary agency responsible for ZEEVIC; the Secretary of Transportation serves on the Council, and MDOT is statutorily required to provide administrative and staff support.
The Director of MEA (or designee) is a statutory member of the Council, and MEA is required to assist MDOT with staffing and support.
The Executive Director of the Technical Staff of the PSC (or designee) is a statutory member of the Council, and the PSC is required to assist MDOT in providing staff support.

The bill amends the Council's composition to explicitly add the Secretary of General Services (or designee) as a member, directly aligning with DGS's responsibilities over state facility charging infrastructure and fleet procurement.

The Secretary of the Environment (or designee) is a designated statutory member of the Council to help integrate zero-emission vehicles into the state's environmental and emissions-reduction frameworks.
The People's Counsel (or designee) is designated as a statutory member of the Council representing residential utility consumers regarding electric vehicle charging and grid impacts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The legislation directly establishes, codifies statutory provisions for, and alters the composition and reporting schedule of an executive advisory body (ZEEVIC).
The Secretary of Planning (or designee) is designated as a statutory member of the Council to advise on land use and infrastructure planning.
The Secretary of Commerce (or designee) is a statutory member of the Council to advise on economic and business impacts related to zero-emission vehicle adoption.
The Governor designates the chair/cochairs of the Council, appoints numerous stakeholder representatives, and receives required interim and final reports.
Assists the Governor in vetting and processing appointments for the diverse stakeholder and industry positions added or clarified on the Council.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes an individual who hunts and harvests an antlerless deer to claim a State income tax credit. Limits the credit to up to $75 of qualified butchering and processing expenses per deer. Requires the individual to donate the processed meat to a 501(c)(3) venison donation program. Caps total annual credits at $300 unless deer are harvested under a deer management permit. Requires participating venison donation programs to report donor information annually to the Comptroller. Terminates the tax credit on June 30, 2029.
qa_results.responsible_party: Comptroller of Maryland
qa_results.stakeholders: Hunters harvesting antlerless deer, 501(c)(3) venison donation programs, and recipients of donated venison
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues decrease by an estimated $175,000 annually in FY 2025 through FY 2029. The Comptroller's Office can implement the bill with existing budgeted resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary agency responsible for administering the state income tax credit for venison donation, receiving mandatory annual donor reports from participating venison donation programs, and managing the resulting reduction in state general fund revenues.

The bill requires that the hunting and harvesting of deer comply with state hunting laws and regulations and references deer management permits to qualify for an exemption to the annual tax credit cap, both of which fall under the Department of Natural Resources' regulatory authority.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Governor to include up to $20,000,000 annually for the comprehensive flood management grant program starting in fiscal 2026. Requires at least 40% of grant funding to support projects located in or directly benefiting underserved or overburdened communities. Applies this targeted funding requirement in fiscal year 2026 and each subsequent fiscal year. Directs unawarded funds at the end of a fiscal year to remain in the program.
